en: Why does Brazil speak Portuguese, when almost all of its neighbors speak Spanish?
I'm Max, and this is Max Wise.
The answer starts with a line drawn across the ocean.
In the late fourteen hundreds, Spain and Portugal were racing to find a sea route to Asia.
Portugal sailed south around Africa, while Spain sent Columbus west.
But it wasn't Asia. It was the Americas.
Both kingdoms wanted the new lands, so they asked the Pope.
In fourteen ninety three, he drew a line from pole to pole, one hundred leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands.
Land to the west went to Spain.
Land to the east went to Portugal.
Portugal wanted more room, so it pushed the line farther west.
In fourteen ninety four, the Treaty of Tordesillas set it at three hundred seventy leagues west of Cape Verde.
Then, in fifteen hundred, Portuguese sailors reached South America.
And its eastern bulge stuck out past the line, right on Portugal's side.
Over the next centuries, Portuguese settlers pushed far beyond that line, deep into the Amazon.
Later treaties drew the borders we see today.
So Brazil speaks Portuguese because of one line drawn on an ocean map.
